title: Why Hands-On Learning Isn’t Always The Best Approach
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler reports on a UK randomized trial of about 2,500 ten- and eleven-year-olds learning evolution, in which a teacher-told story about peppered moths outperformed a hands-on moth-hunting activity, and studying abstract trilobites worked at least as well as modelling human limbs. The result surprised the researchers, who had expected engagement and personal relevance to win. Wexler then uses cognitive science to explain it: explicit instruction works best for novices, hands-on tasks overload working memory, the mind is built for narrative, and writing about what was learned consolidates memory. Teachers in the study could not always tell which approach worked better, which supports her warning that visible engagement is not the same as learning. She does not dismiss hands-on work, only the training-room orthodoxy that it is inherently superior.
points: In a large randomized trial, a story told by the teacher beat a hands-on activity for teaching natural selection, contradicting what both researchers and teachers expected.
Hands-on tasks can swamp working memory so that pupils recall the fun but not the concept.
Narrative is easier to understand and retain, so true stories can be an effective teaching tool in science and history.
Visible engagement is a poor proxy for learning, and teachers in the study were enthusiastic about the activity even when the results did not favour it.
quotes: Do kids learn best from hands-on activities and content that relates to their own experience, as most educators believe? A new study suggests they learn more when teachers tell stories and use examples that are remote from students’ lives.

The researchers found that all students gained a better understanding of evolution, regardless of which lessons they’d been exposed to. But they also found that the students who got a combination of the peppered-moth story and trilobite modeling learned the most, although the difference was not statistically significant.

Most teachers would probably have predicted, like the researchers, that the moth-hunting activity would work best. Education orthodoxy holds that engagement is the key to learning, and hands-on activities appear to engage students more.

Explicit instruction works best unless learners already have quite a bit of information about the topic. Maybe the moth-hunting activity could have effectively reinforced what kids learned from the PowerPoint presentation, but it wasn’t the best way of introducing them to the concept of natural selection.

When kids are being organized into groups, trying to use forceps as bird “beaks,” counting up the moths that are “eaten,” etc., they may not have the cognitive capacity to focus on the point of the lesson. And they may remember how much fun they had hunting moths but not much about natural selection.

As the researchers noted, their findings don’t mean that student engagement is unimportant—just that educators’ expectations about what will engage students aren’t always accurate. And the fact that students are more visibly engaged, as they were during the moth-hunting activity, doesn’t mean they’re learning more.
